turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning. You're a bit behind, the clinic ran over. What's brought you in, Mr Brennan?
[SEG0002] person_2 (PATIENT): The left knee, doctor. It's been giving me gyp, and the job wants a note. Something on paper, like.
[SEG0003] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I'm his wife, Nuala. He's been hobbling about the house a month, easy. Won't admit it.
[SEG0004] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah stop. It's not a month. A fortnight, I'd say. And I'm not hobbling. I just take the stairs a bit slower. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0005] person_1 (DOCTOR): A fortnight to a month, so. We'll not split hairs on the day. Did it swell up, or give way under you?
[SEG0006] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No swelling. It never gave way.
[SEG0007] person_1 (DOCTOR): Any other joints, or is it just that one?
[SEG0008] person_2 (PATIENT): Just the left knee. The right one's grand.
[SEG0009] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He was up a ladder at the weekend painting the hall. I told him not to.
[SEG0010] person_2 (PATIENT): That was a different thing. The knee was at me before the ladder. Sure the hall looks well now.
[SEG0011] person_1 (DOCTOR): Grand, we'll leave the decorating. The nurse took your pressure outside. She read it out, 178 over 102.
[SEG0012] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): I heard her. 178 over 102. She looked a bit shocked, so she did.
[SEG0013] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the white coat. It always goes up in this place. I don't know, doctor, I'm grand at home.
[SEG0014] person_1 (DOCTOR): We'll repeat it in a minute. Before that, any headache, chest pain, or shortness of breath with it?
[SEG0015] person_2 (PATIENT): No. No headaches. No chest pain. I'm not short of breath.
[SEG0016] person_1 (DOCTOR): Sit easy, arm out. Don't talk for a second. Right. I'm getting 164 over 96 on this cuff. Still up, but it's not the nurse's number.
[SEG0017] person_2 (PATIENT): There you are. It drops when I sit. White coat, I'd nearly bet on it.
[SEG0018] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): His father had a stroke. I'm only saying it because you're on about the pressure. Years ago, now.
[SEG0019] person_1 (DOCTOR): That's worth knowing, thank you. Are you on any tablets? Pressure ones, or anything else?
[SEG0020] person_2 (PATIENT): No pressure tablets. I take paracetamol for the knee. Two tablets, when it's bad.
[SEG0021] person_1 (DOCTOR): How often would that be?
[SEG0022] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't know, doctor. Maybe every other day. Not every day, anyway.
[SEG0023] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Most evenings he takes them, if I'm honest. And he had omeprazole for the stomach, but he knocked that on the head.
[SEG0024] person_2 (PATIENT): Yeah I stopped the omeprazole. A few weeks back, myself. The paracetamol isn't most evenings. Only when the knee is niggling.
[SEG0025] person_1 (DOCTOR): So paracetamol when you need it, omeprazole stopped. Any allergy to medicines that you know of?
[SEG0026] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't think so. Nothing I could name. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0027] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): Penicillin. When he was small he came out in a rash. We've kept away from it ever since.
[SEG0028] person_2 (PATIENT): I don't remember that one bit. I've had antibiotics since and I was grand. I don't think I'm allergic.
[SEG0029] person_1 (DOCTOR): I'll note that you and your wife don't agree on the penicillin. I'm not reaching for an antibiotic today either way. Let me see the knee.
[SEG0030] person_1 (DOCTOR): Left knee, bend and straighten. There's a bit of creaking in there. No redness, and I can't see any swelling. Tender on the inner side, though.
[SEG0031] person_2 (PATIENT): That's the bit, yeah. Ow.
[SEG0032] person_1 (DOCTOR): I was going to book an x-ray this morning. But it's early enough, and there's no swelling, so I'll park that.
[SEG0033] person_2 (PATIENT): Whatever you think is best. I don't know, doctor.
[SEG0034] person_1 (DOCTOR): Now the pressure. 164 over 96 here, higher with the nurse, and your father had a stroke. I was going to start amlodipine, 5 milligrams, one every morning.
[SEG0035] person_2 (PATIENT): Ah, do I need a tablet? The chemist did it last month and he said it was grand. Around 130. I don't know the bottom number.
[SEG0036] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): He rang me from the car. 128 over something, he said. He was delighted.
[SEG0037] person_1 (DOCTOR): That changes my mind, so. If it was normal at the chemist, I'm not starting any tablet today. No amlodipine. We'll watch it at home instead.
[SEG0038] person_2 (PATIENT): Grand. I told you it was the white coat.
[SEG0039] person_1 (DOCTOR): It might be white coat, and it might be the start of real high blood pressure. One visit won't tell me which. Home readings will.
[SEG0040] person_3 (FAMILY_MEMBER): We can do that. I'll write them down if he forgets.
[SEG0041] person_2 (PATIENT): I won't forget. I'll do my best. I don't know, doctor, mornings are a rush.
[SEG0042] person_1 (DOCTOR): Morning and evening, sitting, for a week. The monitor can come from reception on your way out. Bring the page back to me.
[SEG0043] person_1 (DOCTOR): Earlier you said no headaches. Is that still right?
[SEG0044] person_2 (PATIENT): Well, actually, I do get a thump in the head some mornings. Not every morning. I wouldn't call it bad. I don't know when it started.

[SEG0045] person_1 (DOCTOR): So there is a mild morning headache, and the start date is a blank. For the knee, keep the paracetamol, ice it if it puffs up, and ease off the stairs and the ladders. We might do a scan if it does not settle.
[SEG0046] person_2 (PATIENT): A scan, is it? Not now?

[SEG0047] person_1 (DOCTOR): Not now. If it's still sore in two weeks we might organise an ultrasound, or an x-ray, whichever fits. Let's see you back in two weeks with the pressure diary, and I'll look at the knee the same day. I'll leave a note at reception, light duties, no heavy lifting and no ladders for the fortnight.

spec.situation: Patient attends for something minor (a knee or a form) and the nurse finds high BP; BP read aloud twice with different numbers; patient says it is white coat; family history of stroke said in passing; no tablets started today, home monitoring arranged.
features: hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.
doctor_changes_mind: the doctor says one plan, then changes it after new information; the label holds the final plan.

denial_then_admission: the patient first denies a symptom, then later describes it. The label records the symptom as present (the later, fuller answer) and does NOT also record the earlier denial as a negative finding.
relative_speaks_for_patient: a relative answers for the patient and the patient partly contradicts; reported_by follows who said it.

bad.reason: 178/102 stated by doctor, but it was the nurse's reading, not doctor's own measurement.

omissions.text: Negative finding omitted: patient denied headaches when first asked about symptoms with the raised blood pressure, before later clarifying he does get mild morning headaches.

Medication plan change not recorded: doctor initially planned to start amlodipine 5 mg once every morning for blood pressure, then explicitly decided not to start it after hearing about the normal chemist reading ('No amlodipine').
Past/home blood pressure reading at the chemist was reported as normal about last month, around 130/unknown diastolic, with wife recalling 128 over something.
Investigation plan not recorded correctly: doctor said he had been going to book a knee x-ray that morning but decided to defer it because it was early and there was no swelling.
